Editorial drafts, to be reviewed for technical accuracy before launch.
Frost, grit, water and floor heating all matter. Appearance alone is not enough.
Porcelain is defined by very low water absorption: 0.5 % or less in the EN 14411 group BIa. Many ceramic wall tiles absorb considerably more, which is why they are normally kept indoors and on walls.
Porcelain is the usual choice for floors, entrances and wet rooms. Glazed ceramic is lighter, easier to cut and offers rich colour for walls and splashbacks.
The name alone is not proof. Choose by the documented values for the exact product: water absorption, breaking strength, slip resistance and, outdoors, frost resistance.
Editorial draft. Verify requirements with the manufacturer and installer. Photograph for mood only.
Multiply length by width for every floor and wall area. Subtract large openings such as doors and big windows.
A common starting point is 10 % for a straight layout and around 15 % for diagonal or patterned layouts. Complex rooms can need more.
Shade and size can vary between production batches. Order everything at once and keep a few spare tiles for later repairs.
Northern daylight changes strongly through the year. Compare a surface in morning, midday and evening light before you decide; the 3D studio lets you move the sun.
One dominant floor surface and one quieter wall surface usually read calmer than three competing materials.
A screen cannot show texture or true colour. Request physical samples before ordering a full project.
Outdoor tiles need documented frost resistance, a drained substrate and a suitable flexible adhesive. Freeze and thaw cycles punish weak details.
Check the declared slip resistance for wet rooms, entrances and steps. Do not judge grip from a photograph.
Stone and porcelain conduct heat well. Follow the adhesive and movement-joint instructions from the installer and manufacturer.
